The king recited the fifth verse to ask the meaning of his words:

5. Who is on Chien Do Gia hill?

The elephant responded through the sixth verse:

6. My mother on Chien Do Gia mountain
Miserable and blind, so sad,
Stamping one foot against the root of an ancient tree,
Because that elephant king is me.

When he heard that, the king immediately gave him freedom, and recited the seventh verse:

7. The heroic elephant takes care of his mother,
Should be set free, just let it be,
Let the elephant go home to his mother
And reunite with his family.

The eighth and ninth verses come from the Supreme Wisdom of the Buddha:

8. Freed from captivity,
No strings attached, king of the forest elephant,
Some words of advice to that king 11,
The elephant returns to the mountainous place.

9. Then down to that cool, clear lake,
The elephant has come here many times,
Using his trunk to suck water from that lake
Splattering all over his mother's body.

But the Bodhisattva's mother thought it was starting to rain, so she recited the tenth verse to blame the rain:

10. Someone brought rain so out of time
What a cruel god, oh my god!
Because now the child is gone,
The child used to take care of me.

At that time the Bodhisattva recited the eleventh verse to reassure his mother:

11. Why are you always lying there, mother!
Here, your child has returned,
The Great Emperor, Sir Thong Tue
Let the child return safely.

The mother immediately responded and thanked the king through the last verse:

12. Long live the Great King!
May you bring back a strong country,
You give me freedom,
To you, I have full respect!

The king was so pleased with the Bodhisattva's virtue that he ordered a town to be built not far from that lake and the king often came to serve the Bodhisattva and his mother. Then, when his mother passed away, he went far away to a monastery called Karandaka. Here five hundred wise men resided and the king often came to make offerings to them. The king ordered a stone statue of the Bodhisattva to be carved and he often came to worship him to show his admiration. Gradually, people from all over Jambudvipa (India) gathered there to celebrate a festival called the Elephant Festival.

When the Master finished speaking, he declared the Truths and recognized the previous life. (Then at the end of the Truths, the Bhikkhu who supported
the mother had settled into the First Fruition (Stuṣuṇī):

- At that time Ànanda was the king, his mother was Mahà Mayà, the elephant mother and it was
I, the elephant king, who raised my mother.

Comment:

Filiality is one of the virtues promoted by the Buddha in his present life as well as in his previous incarnations.

Every time he heard that a Bhikkhu had to support his elderly parents even though he had become a monk and followed the path of liberation, he would praise him and tell a Jataka story to prove that filial piety is one of the virtues that the Bodhisattva, his predecessor, demonstrated in many forms of reincarnation: birds, animals, or humans: The Bodhisattva was a filial robin in the Rice Fields (No. 484), as a filial deer. in the previous Life King Loc rejoices (no. 385), is a filial son in the previous life Sàma (number 540), and is a filial elephant in this previous life.

(Excerpt from the monthly magazine Giac Ngo, No. 77, August 2002)

tom_tat: The story of Prince Yuvanjana (460. Former life of Yuvana) "I pay my respects to the King..." This story was told by the Master while staying at Jetavana about His Great Birth. One day, the Bhikkhus gathered in the Dharma hall: - Dear friend
noi_dung:
The Story of Prince Yuvanjana

(460. Yumànjana's predecessor)

"I pay my respects to the King..."

This story the Master told while staying at Jetavana about His Great Birth. One day, the Bhikkhus gathered in the Dharma hall:
- Dear friends - one Bhikkhu told the other - the former 12 Powered Being
could certainly live at home, could be a Holy Chakravartin King in the middle of the
Great World full of treasures and glory with four supernatural powers, surrounded by
a crowd of more than a thousand monks. However, He gave up all those glorious scenes when He realized the danger that lay in lust. At midnight, along with Channa, he rode his royal horse Kanthaka and left. On the banks of the Anoma River, that glorious river, He said goodbye to the world and for six consecutive years lived an ascetic and self-mortifying life, after which he practiced self-practice and attained Enlightenment.

The monks said this to each other about the Buddha's merits. The Master
stepped in and asked:

- Hey monks, while sitting here, what are you talking about?

The monks told him. The Master said:

- Hey monks, this is not the first time the Tathagata has done a great event
in the world. In the past, he gave up his throne in the kingdom of Ba La Nai, which was twelve miles wide.

After saying that, he told a story from the past.

* * *

Once upon a time, there was a king named Sabbadatta who ruled over the city of Ramma. The capital city that we now call Ba La Nai was called Surundhana in the Udaya Jataka (no. 488), also Sudassana in the Cullasutasoma Jataka (no. 525), or Brahmavaddhana in the Sonandana Jataka (no. 530), and strangely Pupphavati in the Khandahàla Jataka (no. 542). In this Yuvanjana Jataka, it is called Ramma city. So that name changes according to many circumstances.

At that time, King Sabbadatta had a thousand princes, and he appointed Prince Yuvanjana as Viceroy.

Early one morning, the crown prince sat on his splendid royal chariot in an extremely majestic view, leisurely strolling in the royal garden. All over the tops of trees, blades of grass, tips of branches, on spider webs strung across the tips of reeds, he saw dew drops dangling like countless strings of pearls. He asked:

- Hey, friendly driver, what is this?

- Your Highness, this is the liquid that falls during the cold season, which people call morning dew. The Crown Prince continued to travel and have fun in the royal garden all day. In the afternoon, when he returned to the old path, he could no longer see any dew drops. He asked:

- Dear Sir, where are the dew drops? Now we can no longer see them.

The other replied:

- Your Highness, when the sun rises high, the fog melts and sinks to the ground.

Hearing that, the crown prince was disappointed and said:

- Human life is created just like morning dew drops on a blade of grass. We need to be free from the oppressive burden of sickness, old age and death. I have to say goodbye to my parents and leave this world.

Thus, due to the cause of the morning dew drops, he perceives the three realms of existence (Sex Realm, Form Realm, Formless Realm) as if he were in a burning fire. When he returned to the palace, he went to see his father in his magnificent court. After bowing to his father, he stood aside and recited the first verse to ask his father's permission to leave the world:

1. I pay my respects to the King,
Among the royal officials, friends, and ministers,
Your Majesty, I wish to leave this world,
Please do not reject me.

Next, the king recited the second verse to dissuade him:

2. What are your dreams, O Du Van,
I grant you all your wishes,
If anyone harms me, I protect you,
Remember to be a hidden monk.

Hearing that, the prince recited the third verse:

3. No one will harm me,
My dream is fulfilled,
But I want to find a safe place
That old age will not destroy.

The Master recited half a verse to explain this issue:

4. The Crown Prince told his father,
The king immediately told his son,

The second half of the song was recited by the king:

Don't leave this world, my prince,
The people of the capital all mourn.

The prince replied again with this verse:

5. Great Emperor, don't let your children stay away from you
A life without worldliness and vanity,
I'm afraid if you indulge in too many desires
You will become a prey to old age.

When he heard this, his father hesitated. After that, the mother was informed:

- Your Excellency, the crown prince is asking the king's permission to become a monk.

She asked:

- What are you saying?

6. I beg you, my dear child,
And I hope you stay close,
I want to see you always, prince,
Don't leave this mortal world.

When he heard that, the prince recited the seventh verse:

7. Like the tip of a blade of grass, condensed with dew,
When the sun shines brightly,
So is the worldly life,
Please don't stop me, dear mother.

After he said that, she kept begging him, with the aim of stopping him. Then, the Great Being told his father the eighth verse:

8. Tell the people carrying the palanquin, let's lift it together!
Don't let your old mother keep stopping you,
The child wants to enter the Holy Path,
Far from life, birth and death 13, beat Minh Quan!

When the father heard his son speak, he said:

- Dear Queen, please take the palanquin to my Thuong Lac Palace to rest in peace.

At the king's command, the queen's legs collapsed, then she was surrounded by maids to help her leave. When she entered the harem and stood looking towards the Dafa hall, she wondered about her son's news. After his mother left, the Bodhisattva asked his father's permission again. The king could not refuse him, so he immediately said:

- Hey dear prince, just follow your wishes and renounce the worldly world.

When he heard the king's approval of this, Bodhisattva's younger brother, Prince Yudhitthila, came to pay homage to his father, and also asked for permission to follow the monastic life like that, the king immediately agreed.

Both princes said goodbye to their father and now, after renouncing all worldly pleasures, they left the Great Hall in the midst of the crowd. The Chief Queen looked at the Great Master and cried:

- The Crown Prince has left the world, this Ramma capital will be empty.

9. Hurry, pray for happiness, my child!
I'm sure Ram-ma is empty,
The Great Emperor Sab-ba has just approved
Prince Du-van has become a monk.

10. Crown Prince, big brother among thousands,
The prince looks as real as gold,
From now on, the majestic prince
Puts on a golden robe and leaves the world.

Bodhisattvas do not immediately embark on the path of practice. No, first he came to say goodbye to his parents, then with his younger brother, Prince Yudhitthila, he left the capital and told the crowd following them to return, and the two of them headed to the Snow Mountain region. There, the two built a hermitage in a place full of peace and lived the life of a pure sage practicing upward meditation. The two lived their entire lives on wild tubers and fruits and were then born in the Brahma world.

This issue is explained through the last verse derived from the Supreme wisdom of the Buddha:

11. Prince Du-thi and Du-van
Living the pure life of a sage,
Farewell to his father and mother,
Cut in half the chain of Death 14.

* * *

When the Master finished his Dharma talk, he said:

- Monks, this is not the first time the Tathagata has abandoned his kingdom to follow the monastic life, but in the past he also did the same.

Then He recognized the Precursor:

- At that time, the parents of today's royal family were the king's father and mother,
Ànanda was the younger brother Yudhitthila and the crown prince Yuvanjana was Ta.

Comment:

The Great Emergence is the most important topic of the Buddha's Jatakas.

Bodhisattvas, the Buddha's predecessor, can come from the noble circumstances of kings, rich Brahmins, or poor untouchables. I have read many previous lives in which the Bodhisattva came from a royal family and left the palace to practice, like the story of King Susimà leaving when he saw the first gray hair appear.

In this incarnation, crown prince Yuvanjana was in his prime, full of vitality and hope for a glorious future on the throne among thousands of other princes. On an early morning trip, the prince saw morning dew hanging on the trees and grass, but in the afternoon they all disappeared. He was disappointed and compared human life to birth and death like dew drops. Then he decided to find a way to escape life and death. From there, he saw all three worlds as if they were burning in a burning fire, urging him to quickly set out. He immediately went to meet his father and mother to explain his reason for becoming a monk and persuade them to agree to allow him to fulfill his wish.

This worldview was presented by the Buddha right in the third sutta on "burning fire" that he preached after the day of Enlightenment to the assembly of the three Venerable Kassapa (Kasapa), causing all these thousands of disciples who were fire worshipers to attain Arhatship. We also often encounter the view that life is like a drop of dew and the world is burned by the fire of greed, anger, and ignorance in many Dharma verses.

Furthermore, this concept is also highlighted as unique features through two typical sutras of Mahayana (Development) Buddhism, the Diamond Sutra and the Lotus Sutra. Thus we can see the consistent view of the Three Dharma Seals of everything that exists in the world in the teaching systems of Buddhism from time immemorial to the present.

(Excerpt from Giac Ngo monthly magazine, No. 74, May 2002)

tieu_de: Story of the Auspicious Ancient Śāla Tree
tom_tat: The story of Sàla, the auspicious Ancient Tree (465. Bhadda - Sàla's predecessor) "Who are you standing in the middle of space..." This story was told by the Master while staying at Jetavana (Ky Vien) about doing good deeds towards his relatives. At that time, King Vidudabha had just succeeded
noi_dung:
The story of Sàla, the auspicious ancient tree

(465. Bhadda - Sàla's predecessor)

"Who are you standing in the middle of space..."

This story was told by the Master while staying at Jetavana (Ky Vien) about doing
good deeds towards his relatives.
At that time, King Vidudabha, who had just succeeded his father, Pasenadi, in Kosala, decided
to send soldiers to kill the Shakyamuni family to avenge his old hatred towards
foreign people. When the Buddha heard the news, he immediately went to Kapilavatthu city to
prevent the king from marching there.

On the day the Master returned from his third departure, after traveling for alms,
and having finished eating, he was resting in the Incense Room, Sangha
from everywhere gathered in the Dharma Hall. When sitting together, the Sangha began to talk about the merits of the Master.

- Dear Sages, the Master only needs to appear and make the king retreat, that is
Resolved His relatives from the fear of death. The Master is truly a good friend, always helping the family.

The Master came in and asked the Sangha what they were talking about while sitting
there. The monks responded to Him. Then, He said:

- Monks, it is not only now that Tathagata acts for the benefit
of his relatives, but in the past Tathagata also did so.

Along with these words, He told a story from the past.

* * *

Once upon a time, when King Brahmadatta reigned in Benares, and practiced the Ten Kingly Dharmas (Ten Virtues of a Wise King), he thought to himself: "All over this world of Jambudvipa, kings and lords live in palaces supported by many pillars. So a palace supported by many pillars is not miraculous, but what if I build a palace with only one pillar supporting it?... At that time I will become the greatest king among them. king!". So he summoned the architects and told them to build him a magnificent palace built on just one pillar. They said:

- Please obey

Then they went deep into the forest.

There, they admired many tall, straight trees worthy of being the only pillar of such a luxurious palace. They said to each other: - Here there are enough trees of this type, but the road is rough, we can never carry them with us, so we must consult the king about that.

When they said so, the king replied:

- Use a hook or anchor to pull them back, it'll be even faster.

But they answered:

- No hook can do this.

The king said:

- Then find a tree in my palace.

The builders went into the royal garden, where they saw a noble, straight Sala tree with luxuriant branches and leaves, still revered by villagers and townspeople, even the royal family often came to worship and make offerings. They immediately reported to the king. Afraid to judge:

They replied:

- Please obey.

They came to the royal garden, their hands full of fragrant garlands and other spices, then hung on the tree a garland of five bunches, coiled a rope around the tree trunk, tied a bouquet of fragrant flowers to it, then lit incense lamps, worshiped and prayed clearly:

- From now until the next seven days, we will chop down the tree according to the king's orders. May the Gods residing in this tree go somewhere else, and it's not our fault.

The deity living on the tree heard this and thought to himself: "These builders are determined to cut down the tree and destroy my residence. Now my life will only last as long as this residence lasts. All the young Sala trees surrounding this tree, with many of my relatives residing, will also be destroyed. The destruction of myself is not as important as the destruction of my descendants. So I must protect my life. them".

So at midnight, with a splendid and majestic outfit, the Tree God entered the king's splendid palace, shining brightly throughout the room and stood crying next to the king's pillow. He was very frightened when he saw the god and immediately uttered the first verse:

1. Who are you, standing in the middle of space,
Dressed like a god,
Why does that terror arise,
Why are your eyes filled with tears?

Hearing that, the lord of the Tree Spirit recited two verses:

2. In the kingdom, O king,
You know the name of the tree: Dai Cat Tuong,
It has been standing for sixty thousand years,
All the people worship me.

3. Although they built many cities,
Royal palaces, royal palaces,
Yet they did not bother us at all,
Nor did they cause us any harm,
Because they worshiped us so much,
May you, Lord, also honor us!

Next, the king recited two other verses:

4. But this great tree trunk,
I have never seen before,
The circumference is beautiful, even the height,
Powerful, what a sturdy tree.

5. I want to build a beautiful palace,
Only need a single pillar as its base,
I want to place you there,
Your life is not short, my God.

Hearing that, the Lord recited two verses:

6. Since you wish to chop down the sacred tree,
Please cut me into small pieces,
And cut this body piece by piece,
Or don't do anything, cut Anh Quan.

7. First cut off the top of the head,
Next the middle, the root next,
If you can cut me down like that,
Death will no longer cause suffering.

After that, the king recited two verses again:

8. First of all the limbs, next to the nose and ears,
When the person in distress is pregnant and dying,
Finally this head falls,
This death is painful.

9. Ancient auspicious tree! Lord of the forest!
What pleasure do you feel?
Why, what reason do you desire
The tree trunk to be cut into pieces?

The great auspicious tree immediately responded through two verses:

10. For this noble reason,
Why do I want to cut this body,
Dividing it into pieces, Your Majesty,
Please listen to what I have to say.

11. All around us are prosperous relatives,
Growing thanks to the perfect shelter,
If we fall hard and crush them,
The pain will be overwhelming.

After hearing this, the king was filled with joy: "This God is so noble, he did not want his relatives to lose their shelter due to him losing his own residence. So he acted for the benefit of his kin."

And the king recited the last verse:

12. Ancient Cat Tuong, Lord of the forest!
Your thoughts are truly noble,
You want to help your relatives,
So I will let you out of fear.

The Lord God, after finishing preaching to the king, immediately left. And the king relied on his advice, gave alms and did many other good deeds until he died and went to live with the assemblies in Heaven.

* * *

After finishing this Dharma talk, the Master said:

- Monks, in this way the Tathagata still acts for the benefit of his
self and relatives.

Then He recognized the Precursor:

- At that time Ānanda was the king, the Buddha's assembly were the gods residing
in the saplings of the Sāla tree, and I was the auspicious ancient tree, the
Lord.

Comment:

Compassion is one of the most important virtues of Buddha and therefore Buddhism is called the Religion of Compassion and Wisdom.

The Buddha taught his disciples to practice compassion for all living beings and the precept of non-killing is the first precept of lay disciples. Not only towards living creatures, He also extended his compassion to all kinds of plants and trees. He advised his disciples not to harm trees, especially forests, which are shelters and good friends of monks. He advised everyone to show gratitude to the noble trees that protected them by not cutting branches to pick leaves. He even told the monks to be careful when pouring leftover food into empty spaces to avoid harming the plants.

In some Samyutta Nikaya suttas, the Buddha taught the masses to do good deeds such as building bridges and roads, planting parks, planting forests, digging wells... to bring about common benefits in this life and rebirth in good realms in the next life. This Jataka story is an example of the compassion of the Bodhisattva, the Buddha's previous incarnation, when he was a tree god.

The king in this story has the ambition to own the most magnificent and unique palace in the world, so he plans to cut down the first ancient Sala tree in the royal garden. That is something that no king has thought of since ancient times because this tree has been revered and worshiped by people across the city for thousands of years, so it may have created a special beauty in the royal garden, bringing peace to visitors every time they visit this scene.

The felling of this ancient tree will seriously affect the surrounding vegetation. But with the humble power of a tree god, the Bodhisattva could do nothing to protect his relatives and friends other than to beg the king to stop that disastrous destruction.

Faced with the noble sacrifice of the tree god, the king suddenly woke up and gave up the idea of ​​cutting down trees to protect the forest as before. From then on, the king followed the advice of the tree god to do good deeds and was born in heaven.

Buddha's advice on protecting the natural environment has never been as practical and necessary as it is in modern times, while all over the world, deforestation still takes place every day, especially primeval forests, causing devastation that seriously affects the lives of all species and threatens even the existence of humanity on this green planet. All of these events stem from the selfish ambitions of people who do not know how to think about the benefits and right to life of others, let alone all living creatures.

(Excerpt from the monthly magazine Giac Ngo, No. 75, June 2002)

tom_tat: The story of Great King Bhallàtiya (504. Former incarnation of Bhallàtiya) "Once upon a time there was the great king Bhallà ...", This story was told by the Master while staying at Jetavana (Ky Vien) about Queen Mallika (Ma Loi) aka Princess Vu Quy Hoa. One day, the story goes:
noi_dung:
The Story of Great King Bhalàtiya

(504. Bhallàtiya Precursor)

"Once upon a time there was the great emperor Bhalla...",

This story the Master told while staying at Jetavana (Ky Vien) about
Queen Mallika (Ma Loi) or Princess Vu Quy Hoa.

One day, the story goes that there was a dispute between the queen and king
Pasenadi of Kosala, about the rights in the palace life, the king became angry
and did not want to see her face. She thought: "I'm sure the Tathagata doesn't know that
the king is angry with me."

When the Master learned about that, the next day, he went to beg for alms in Ba
La Nai with the Sangha following him, then went to the palace gate. The King came out to welcome Him and took His alms bowl, took Him up to the upper floor, invited the Sangha to sit in the appropriate order, then offered welcoming water and food.upper stomach. After the meal, the king sat down to one side. The Master asked:

- Why didn't Queen Mallika come?

The king replied:

- Just because of her foolish pride about her glory.

The Master said:

- Hey Great King, once upon a time, a long time ago, when Your Majesty was still a
male fairy, Your Majesty left his spouse for just one night, but after that he continued to
mourn those seven hundred years.

Then at the king's request, he told a story from the past.

* * *

Once upon a time there was a king named Bhallàtiya who ruled in Ba La Nai. Due to his passion for the wild venison meat smoking on the fire, he was afraid to entrust the kingdom to the great ministers. Then, armed with all five weapons and a pack of refined, intelligent hunting dogs, he left the capital and headed to the Tuyet Son region. He kept traveling along the Ganges River until he could no longer climb any higher, so he followed a tributary a few more miles, killing deer and wild boar while enjoying that grilled meat, until he climbed to a peak.

There is a poetic stream flowing down the whole area, the water is chest high, but in the dry seasons it only reaches the knees. At that time, schools of fish and turtles of all kinds were splashing about, the sand strip under the water was shining like silver, the trees on both banks were drooping and heavy with fruits, birds, bees and butterflies were passionately sucking up ripe fruit juice and honey, flying around in the shade of the shady trees. Here, herds of deer of all kinds were always hanging around. At that time, on the bank of this beautiful stream, there was a pair of fairies holding each other tightly, lovingly caressing each other, then suddenly burst out crying and wailing extremely pitifully. 15.

While the king climbed to the top of Gandhamàdana (Huong Son) along this stream, he suddenly noticed that pair of fairies. "Why do they keep crying and wailing like this?", he thought, "I want to ask why". He only needed to glance at the hunting dogs and snap his fingers. The purebred dogs saw this sign and immediately understood their part, immediately crawled under the bushes and lay close to the ground. As soon as he saw that they had disappeared, he placed his bow and arrows and other weapons next to a nearby tree and crept gently closer to the pair of fairies so that no one could hear their footsteps, then he asked:

- Why do you mourn?

To explain this, the Master recited three verses:

1. Once upon a time there was the great emperor Bhallà,
He still went hunting far away,
Climbed all the way to Huong Son and suddenly saw
Full of flowers blooming with demons.

2. He ordered the dogs to all lie still
Put the bows and arrows on the ground
Step forward to deliver the greeting
Over there, I just saw a pair of fairies:

3. "Winter has passed, why do you come back
to chat and chat next to the mountains?
Why are you so human-like?
What kind of species do you call, tell me?"

Hearing the king's question, the male fairy said nothing, but the female fairy responded as follows:

4. Tam Dinh, Hoang Son, Mount Malaysia 16,
The gods followed the cool stream, crossed,
The wild animals thought they were real people,
But the hunters called ghosts.

Next, the king recited three verses:

5. You are as affectionate as lovers,
But you cry so bitterly,
The fairies are like worldly people,
Why do you mourn, please explain!

6. You caress like lovebirds,
But cry full of sorrow and sadness,
The couple is no different from worldly people,
Why are you so sad? Tell the wall!

7. Like lovers, they keep caressing,
But the crying is so long,
You look like worldly people,
Why are you so sad? Tell me!

The following verses are due to the two sides responding to each other:

Fairy:

8. You and I spent a night apart,
Without love, heavy with sadness,
Longing, but
We can never return that night.

King:

9. Why did you lie so lonely that night
It made you moan in sadness?
The young couple looked like worldly people,
Lost money, or did the old woman die?

Fairy:

10. Over there, the shade, the stream gushed out
Between the rocks, then the storm blew through,
Because he was so anxious to find me
The lover waded across the shore.

11. While my feet are throbbing,
I go looking for thousands of flowers and herbs
To make bracelets for my beloved boy
And me, just when I see him again.

12. Make a bunch of yellow bells, green grass,
Cool white daffodils filled with dew
Give your beloved an antique wreath
With me, just when you meet your partner.

13. Then I picked a bouquet of roses
The most beautiful flowers in the area,
To tie him and me together
Wreaths around their necks, when they meet.

14. Next to the flowers and leaves, I went to find them
And spread them all over the soft ground,
Where all night long, sharing the same pillow and dreaming,
The couple slept peacefully.

15. Cinnamon wood and agarwood followed,
Placing it on a stone, I crushed it,
Making incense all over my beloved
And me, the scent is so magical!

16. Standing on the bank of a flowing stream,
I picked lotus flowers until the end:
At dusk, that stream overflowed everywhere,
If I want to go to that bank, I can't wait!

17. We had to stand both on each shore,
Looking at each other earnestly, waiting to pass by,
Oh, so many cries and laughter,
That night was filled with pain and sorrow!
18. In the morning, the winter sesame trees had grown high,
When they saw the stream drying up quickly,
You and I hurriedly walked, hugging each other tightly,
Immediately laughing and crying together!

19. Nearly seven hundred years, only three missing,
Since you and I had to separate,
My heart is broken and the sadness of separation
It feels like a lifetime!

King:

20. How long is your life?
If this story has been passed down from ancient times,
Or if many elders say it,
Don't be afraid, tell me.

Fairy:

21. A thousand beautiful, peaceful summers,
Not subject to much suffering,
Scarcely sad, full of ecstasy,
A lifetime filled with happiness and love!

When the king heard that, he thought: "These creatures are lower than humans, yet they still cry and mourn for seven hundred years because of just one night of separation from each other. Not to mention I, the lord of a country three hundred miles wide, had to leave all that glorious scene behind to wander in the wild mountains and forests. What a serious mistake."

He immediately returned. When he arrived at Ba La Nai, the court asked him if he had seen anything rare in the Tuyet Son area. He told the congregation the whole strange story, and from then on he practiced almsgiving and enjoyed his glory.

To explain this, the Master recited the following verse:

22. Thanks to the advice of the pair of fairies,
The Great King immediately returned to his path,
gave up hunting and supported the poor and needy,
Enjoying the days of flying lightly.

And he recited two more verses:

23. Learn the lesson of that fairy,
Don't quarrel, but correct your habits,
Lest you be sad like them
For the rest of your life, because of delusion.

24. Take the lesson from the fairies right away,
Don't argue, but correct your habits,
Lest you suffer like them
All your life, because of your own mistakes.

25. Now, dear Saint,
With a submissive heart and ready obedience,
I hear the golden words
Full of good intentions, filled with kindness,
Countless blessings from the Venerable Master!
As soon as you admonish, your worries immediately disappear!

From then on, the king of Kosala lived in harmony with the queen forever.

* * *

When this Dharma talk ended, the Master recognized the Previous Life:

- At that time, the king of Kosala was a male fairy, queen Mallika was a female fairy and I was King Bhallàtiya.

Comment:

Harmony between people in the family and in society is one of the important topics of the Jataka Tales of the Buddha. In the Singalovada Sutra (Singalovada Sutra) of the Digha Nikaya, the Buddha clearly stated the moral standards for a true person in the world through the example of worshiping the six directions in the law of the Saints.

This sutta clearly states the Buddha's concern for lay life. He advised everyone to live temperately with themselves and maintain cordial, harmonious and mutually respectful relationships between teachers - students, parents - children, husband - wife, friends - friends, master - servant, homeowner and monks.

This is a sutra that promotes the virtuous characteristics of the home life. And these characteristics are deployed through many rich and vivid forms in this Jataka Tales. All bonds of affection that unite people in the family and in society are praised. In particular, emotional harmony in a couple's life is also encouraged by the Buddha through many Jataka stories such as: number 223: the story of Food on the go, number 320: the story of Easy Giving, number 333: the story of the Gecko, number 489: the story of Queen Suruci, and 519: the story of Queen Sambulà... for all types of people from ordinary people to kings.

In this case, the Buddha reconciled the dispute between King Pasenadi (Ba Tu Nac) and Queen Mallikà (Ma Loi) by telling the story of King Bhallàtiya, a king who was too indifferent to both state and household affairs, so he left the court and was engrossed in hunting and hunting in the jungle until one day he happened to meet a pair of fairies who were amorous creatures who always lived together, so they were only separated for one night. They mourned and suffered all their lives, lasting thousands of years!

This strange meeting made the king realize his mistake in neglecting the main affairs of the country, with the large family in the inner palace waiting day and night for his return to fulfill the king's duty to all people.

In conclusion, the Buddha also advised King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika to stop arguing and hurt each other and learn the habit of yielding to bring peace to themselves and everyone around them. Then this royal couple expressed their repentance by practicing a lifestyle in harmony with the ancient saying:

"One abstinence is equal to nine good deeds".

Thus we can see that in addition to the Six Harmony principles that the Buddha taught the Sangha to always practice in their holy life, the Singalovada Sutta and the Jataka stories are full of human love and religion, promoting the Buddha's deep concern for life in the family and in society, different from the misconception that Buddhism advocates separation from the world and disregarding everyday life with all its important issues. it.

(Excerpt from the monthly magazine Giac Ngo, No. 80, November 2002)

tom_tat: The story of the wise man Suppàraka (463. Suppàraka's previous life) "Those people had sharp noses like knives..." This story was told by the Master while staying at Jetavana about the perfection of Supreme Wisdom. One day, we heard that, about the evening, the Bhikkhus
noi_dung:
The Story of the Wise Suppàraka

(463. Predecessor Suppàraka)

"Those people have sharp noses like knives..."

This story the Master told while staying at Jetavana about the perfection of the
Supreme Wisdom.

One day, we heard that, in the evening, the Bhikkhus were waiting for
the Tathagata to preach the Dharma to the Sangha, and while sitting in the Dharma Hall, they said to each other:

- Hey Bhikkhu, the Master truly has great wisdom! Vast wisdom! Intellectual diligence, Intellect flexible! Exquisite intelligence! Profound wisdom! Wisdom
He responds to the right place at the right time! Wisdom is as vast as the world, like the endless ocean, like the vast expanse of the sky: throughout the land of Jambudvipa [1] there is no
wise man who can compare with the Ten Powers[2] , like a wave
rising on the ocean that cannot reach the shore, or if it touches the shore,
The other wave will break. Likewise, no one can attain the wisdom of
the Ten Powers, or if he comes to the feet of the Teacher he will be shattered.

With those words, the Sangha praised the supreme wisdom of the Ten Powers.
The Master entered and asked:

- Hey monks, what are you talking about while sitting here?

The monks told him. He said:
- It is not only now that the Tathagata is full of wisdom. In the past, even when his wisdom had not yet reached Enlightenment, he was already wise and intelligent. Even though
he was blind, he also knew through the signs of each ocean that in
that ocean there were hidden gems of all kinds.

Then He told a story from the past.

* * *

Once upon a time, a king named Bharu ruled in the kingdom of Bharu. There is a town by the harbor named Bharukacha or Bharu Lagoon. At that time, Bodhisattva was born into the family of a sea captain there. He was very lovely, with yellow-brown skin. His parents named him Suppàraka - Kumàra.

He grew up with unusually excellent abilities, and even when he was only sixteen years old, he completely mastered the art of navigation. Then when his father passed away, he led a group of sailors and devoted himself to the maritime profession. He was very intelligent and wise. Once he boarded the ship, no ship could harm him.

Over time, he was injured by salt water and lost sight in his eyes. After that incident, even though he was the captain of the sailors, he no longer pursued a commercial career, but decided to serve the king. He came to see the king for that purpose, and the king appointed him the position of juror to evaluate the treasures. From there he determined the value of precious elephants, precious gems and jewels.

One ​​day, an elephant was presented to the king. Its skin was the color of black stone, so it could be used as a king's statue. The king glanced at the elephant and ordered it to be presented to the wise man. The servant brought the animal to meet him. He touched the elephant's entire body and said:

- This elephant does not deserve to be a national symbol. It has the characteristics of an animal with a deformed rear. When the mother elephant gave birth to it, she was not strong enough to carry it on her shoulders, so she let it sit on the ground, so it had a disability in its hind legs.

They questioned those who brought the elephant, and they answered that the wise man had spoken the truth. When the king heard this story, he was very happy and ordered to give the wise man eight gold coins. Another day, people offered a horse to be the king's horse. This animal is also led to the wise. He touched the horse's body with his hand and said:

- This animal is not suitable to be the king's horse. On the day it was born, the mother horse died, so due to lack of mother's milk, it did not grow fully.

His words are also true. When he heard that, the king was very pleased and told him to give him another eight coins.

On another day, a car was brought to be used as a chariot. The king also brought this carriage to you. He touched the car with his hand and said:

- This car is made of hollow wood, so it is not suitable for the king.

This statement of his is as true as the others. The king was once again pleased to hear this story, so he gave him another eight coins. Once again, someone offered the king a precious carpet of great value, and the king immediately brought it to him as before. He touched the carpet all over, then said:

- Here there is a place where the mouse has bitten a hole.

They looked carefully and saw that place, so they immediately told the king. The king was pleased and told him to give him another eight coins.

At that time, the wise man thought: "I only have eight gold coins to see such miraculous things. This is a gift to the barber, this king must be a boy who often cuts hair! Why should I serve such a king? I will return to my own home." So he returned to the port of Bharukaccha and lived there.

At that time, some merchants prepared a boat and were looking for a captain. They thought: "That clever Mr. Suppàraka is a talented wise man. With him on board, no ship will harm him anymore. Even though he is blind, the wise man Suppàraka is still an excellent person." So they went to him and asked him to be captain.

- Dear Friends - He replied - I am blind, how can I steer your boat?

- Venerable Sir, you are indeed blind - The merchants said - but you are the most talented person. Because they kept begging him endlessly, he finally agreed.

- As you told me this, he said - then I will be your captain.

Afterwards, he boarded their boat.

They sailed out into the middle of the ocean. For seven days straight, the boat sailed without any mishap, then an unseasonable wind arose. The boat drifted for four months in the wild ocean, until it reached a place called Khuramàla sea (Sharp Knife Beach). Here, the fish has a human-like body with a sharp snout like a knife blade, tumbling underwater. The merchants observed this fish, asked this Great Sea Master what his name was, and recited the first verse:

1. That group of people's noses are as sharp as knives,
Jumping up high and somersaulting
Let's talk. Suppà, tell us,
By what name is this sea known?

The Great Master heard this sentence, immediately reviewed his sailor knowledge in his mind, and then replied with the second verse:

2. Hey traders of Bharka port
Looking for gold and silver to sell long distances,
This is the Khura sea,
Your boat has lost its way.

At that time, this ocean had many diamonds. The Great Being thought that if he told his friends that this was a sea of ​​diamonds, they would sink the ship because they were greedy for too many diamonds, so he said nothing; but after bringing the boat, he took a rope and let down the net as if to catch fish. With this rope, he picked up a bunch of diamonds and hid them in the boat, then he chose the things of little value and threw them into the sea.

The boat passed through this sea, arriving at another sea called Aggimàla (Fire Area). This sea radiates light as if a fire were burning, like the sun at noon. The merchants asked him through this verse:

3. Behold the ocean like a red flame,
Like the sun shining, we look,
Suppa, please tell my friends,
Can you give me a name?

The Great Being responded to them through the next verse:

4. Hey merchants in Bharka,
Looking for gold and silver to sell over long distances,
This is the sea of Aggi,
Your boat has gone astray.

Now this sea was filled with gold, as before, he took up a bunch of gold and put it on the boat. Crossing this sea, the boat goes to a sea called Dadhimàla (Pound of curd), sparkling like fresh milk or curd. The merchants again asked the name of the sea through verse:

5. Behold, the sea is as white as fresh milk,
White as looking at a puddle of curdled milk,
Suppà, tell your friends,
What is the name of the sea?

The Great Being replied to his friends with the next verse:

6. Hey merchants in Bharka,
Looking for gold and silver to sell over long distances,
This is the Dadhi sea,
Your boat has gone astray.

In this sea there is a lot of silver. He took the silver in the same way as before, and put it on the ark. The boat passed through this sea and reached an ocean called Nilavannakusamàla (Kusa Grass), shaped like a black kusa grass (auspicious grass) or a rice field. The merchants again asked the name of the sea through verses:

7. Behold, the sea is as green as auspicious grass,
It's like looking at a fragrant rice field,
Suppà, tell your friends,
What is the name of the ocean?

He answered through the next verse:

8. Hey merchants of Bharka,
Looking for gold and silver to sell over long distances,
This ocean is Kusa,
Your boat has gone astray.

At that time there were many precious jade in this sea. Just like before, he took a bunch and stored them on the boat. Crossing this sea, the boat goes to a sea called Nalamàla (Reed Beach), shaped like a reed beach or a bamboo forest. The merchants asked the name of the sea through verses:

9. Behold, the ocean is like a clump of reeds,
It's no different than a grove of bamboo,
Suppà, tell your friends,
What is the name of this ocean?

The Great Being responded through the following verse:

10. Hey merchants of Bharka,
Looking for gold and silver to sell long distances,
This sea is called Nala,
Your boat has lost its way.

At that time, this sea was full of corals the color of bamboo clusters, so he scooped up a bunch and put them on the ship. After passing through the Nalamala Sea, the traders came to a sea called Valabhamukha (Basin). Here the water recedes and rises on one side, and so the water recedes on all sides and rises up the vertical cliffs, leaving an area like a deep hole. A wave surged up on one side, like a wall: I heard a terrible roar, as if it would puncture my eardrums or break my heart. Upon seeing this scene, the merchants were frightened and asked the name of the sea through verse:

11. Hey, listen to that terrifying scream,
From the sea, it's so extraordinary!
The deep lake, look, many waves
Rising up steeply like a mountainside,
Suppà, tell your friends,
What is the name of the ocean?

The Bodhisattva responded through verse:

12. Hey merchants of Bharka,
Looking for gold and silver to sell over long distances,
Valabhà this ocean,
Your boat has gone astray.

He continued:

- Dear Friends, once the boat enters this Valabhamukha sea, it cannot return. If this boat goes in there, it will sink and be destroyed.

Now there are seven hundred lives on this boat, they are all afraid of death; so they simultaneously uttered an extremely pitiful cry, like the screams of those burning in the deepest hell. (Infinite Hell). The Great Being thought to himself: "Except me, no one can save their lives. I am determined to save them with an oath of truth." Then he said loudly:

- Dear friends, quickly bathe me with fragrant water, put on new clothes for me, prepare a bowl full of water and stand me in front of the boat.

They all quickly did so. The Great Being held a full cup of water in both hands, stood in front of the boat, performed a prayer for the truth, and recited the last verse:

13. Since I clearly remember my body,
The first wisdom gradually arises,
Not a single person I have killed
This is something I already know clearly,
If this prayer is true,
I hope the boat will return to a place of eternal peace.

For the past four months, the boat that had been traveling in distant seas now seemed to be endowed with supernatural powers, so in just one day it returned to the port of Bharukaccha, all the way to the mainland until it stopped in front of the captain's house, after jumping over a distance of about eleven hundred cubits (1 cubit = 45cm). The Great Being distributed to the merchants all the gold, silver, pearls, coral, diamonds and treasures:

- This amount of treasure is enough for you, so don't travel by sea anymore.

Then he preached the Dharma to them and when he had completed his almsgiving and good deeds throughout his life, he went up to live with the heavenly assembly. * * *

After finishing this Dharma talk, the Master said:

- Hey monks, in the past Tathagata was as wise as he is now.

And He recognized the Precursor:

- At that time, the Buddha's Assembly was an assembly of merchants and I was the Wise Suppàraka.

Comment:

The Buddha's perfect wisdom is one of the most important themes of the Jataka stories.

His transcendent wisdom is presented in very simple forms such as in No. 387 - The Needle Story, when the Bodhisattva is a poor metal salesman with an unparalleled talent for making a delicate needle; or in number 515 - The Story of Sambhava, when he was just a seven-year-old boy, he knew how to explain the issue of Truth and Goodness to the whole court of kings, officials and people. Gradually, the Bodhisattva's wisdom reached its peak when he compared his true eloquence with a number of kings and pagan wise men until finally he won the admiration of his opponents as in numbers 545 - The Story of the Wise Vidhura, and number 546 - The Story of the Great Tunnel, which are the most outstanding long stories of the Jataka series.

After the storm, their boat drifted into unfamiliar and dangerous oceans, but he still clearly knew the characteristics and names of each sea and the different types of treasure in each area. However, he always knew just enough and did not want to take too many treasures lest something unexpected happen.

And finally, when the boat drifted into a vortex that seemed like it would be destroyed, he used all the power of a person who lived righteously all his life to swear an oath of truth to save the entire crew. After his safe return, he distributed all his assets to them and advised them to retire to live a family life practicing good deeds that benefit everyone and themselves.

(Excerpt from the monthly magazine Giac Ngo, No. 81, December 2002)

The Tale of Canda's Couple Songs

(999. Canda Kinnara's predecessor)

"My life is surely about to end...",

The Master told this story while staying at Bo De Lam near Kapilapura, about
Ràhula's mother when she was still in the palace.

While he was sitting in his father's palace, during the meal, the Master told the
Body of Mahàdhammàpàla (number 447) and after the meal was over, he said:

- We want to praise the noble virtues of mother Rahula (Rahula)
right in her interior by telling this Canda Kinnara.

After handing over the alms bowl to his father, he and his two great disciples walked through
the palace of his mother Rahula. At that time, there were forty thousand palace maids who were good at singing and dancing to accompany her, of which one thousand and ninety were daughters of the Sat-di line. When she heard the news that the Tathagata was coming to visit, she came
commanded all of these palace maids to wear yellow robes and the congregation obeyed.

The Master entered and sat down in the seat reserved for him. At that time, the entire congregation of women let out a loud cry and wailed loudly. After letting
the tears flow, Rahula's mother tried to suppress her sadness, stood up
to pay respects to the Master and sat down with the utmost respect for a
king. At that time, His father began to talk about her virtues:

- Dear World-Honored One, please listen. When she heard that the Blessed One had put on the yellow robe,
she also put on the yellow robe, the Blessed One removed all the garlands and jewelry, she
also left everything and just lay down and sat on the ground. When the World-Honored One became a monk, she immediately became an aunt and refused all the gifts that other princes sent her. Her heart was always loyal to the World-Honored One.
Thus, His father recounted all her virtues in many
ways. The Master immediately said:

- Dear Father, it is not strange that today, in the last life of the Tathagata,
This princess loved and maintained loyalty to Tathagata and
only wanted to be guided by Tathagata alone. Indeed, even when
she was born as a non-human species, she remained loyal to her husband
only.

Then, at the request of his father, he told a story from the past.

* * *

Once, when King Brahmadatta reigned in Ba La Nai, the Great Being was born in the Snow Mountain region as a Kinnara Immortal (Khannara: Ca Than) named Canda or Nguyet Lang, his wife was Candà or Nguyet Nga. Both of them lived together on a silver mountain called Candapabbata or Nguyet Quang.

While enjoying the dish, the king suddenly remembered where the small stream was, so he started climbing the hill. At that time, the pair of fairies living on top of Nguyet Son often stayed in the mountain during the rainy season, and only went down the mountain during the dry season. Just then, the male fairy Canda and his wife descended the mountain and walked around. The pair of fairies soaked in perfume, ate pollen, wore inner and outer clothes made of silk woven from flowers, swayed among the vines, and happily sang in a voice as sweet as honey.

The male fairy gradually approached this stream and at a stop beside the stream, he walked down with his wife and sprinkled flowers all over the stream surface while playing in the water. When both of them had finished putting on their floral clothes, on a patch of white sand, shining like a sheet of silver, they spread flowers as a bed and lay down. Having just picked up a piece of bamboo, the male fairy began to play the flute, singing sweetly like honey into his ears, while the female fairy waved her soft hands, dancing and singing nearby.

The king heard the singing, immediately walked on tiptoe so that no one could hear his footsteps, and came close to admire the fairy couple from a discreet hiding place. The king suddenly fell in love with the fairy and thought to himself: "I want to shoot that guy and live here with his wife." Then the king immediately shot and seriously injured the male fairy Canda. He painfully uttered four verses:

1. Surely my life is about to end,
My blood is flowing rapidly, overflowing,
I'm gradually losing all my vitality,
My breath is barely breathing, my dear!

2. I am drowning in pain,
My heart is burning,
But because of your sadness, Moon,
My heart feels unpredictable.

3. Like grass and trees, I keep fading,
Withering like a stream drying up,
My heart is full of emotions, Can-da,
Because of your own sadness.

4. Tears flow from my eyes
Like rain from the foot of a mountain flowing into a lake,
Because my heart is full of compassion,
For your sadness, O Nguyet Nga!

The Great Being lamented like that through four verses while writhing on the flower bed, then lost consciousness and turned his face away. The king still stood in the hiding place. And the nymph did not know that the Great Being had just been injured. Even when he cried like that, she also did not know, because she was intoxicated with her joy. But when she saw him turn away and lie motionless, she began to wonder what had happened to her husband. Rushing to observe her husband, she saw blood flowing from the wound, so unable to bear the terrible pain of her beloved husband's situation, she screamed loudly.

"The male fairy must have died", the king thought to himself and stepped out to reveal himself. When the nymph Candà saw the king, she thought to herself: "This must be the robber who killed my beloved husband", and she ran away trembling. Once standing on the top of the hill, she harshly accused the king through five verses:

5. Oh poor me, cruel lord!
Your family shot and seriously wounded him,
Now he lies there, on the cold ground,
Under a tree, in the middle of thousands of mountains.

6. Prince! This heart-wrenching sadness,
I hope the Queen Mother will pay for it!
The sadness is crushing my heart,
When I see that my lover is dead.

7. Prince! This heart-wrenching sadness,
I hope the queen will pay for it!
The sadness is breaking my heart
When I see that the guy I love is dead.

8. I hope the queen mother will cry for her father now,
And later she will have to cry for her son,
Who, because of lust, is doing evil
For my own husband, it is unjust.

9. I hope the queen has to wait
The situation of losing both her son and her husband
The one who, because of greed, did evil
Let him be innocent, the husband.

After she cried out like that through the five verses above, the king, standing on the top of the mountain, spoke to comfort her through another verse:

10. Don't cry, don't be sad,
I'm sure the night forest blinds your eyes:
The king's palace gives you happiness,
She is the king's queen!

- What did you just say?

The fairy Candà screamed when she heard this, and she answered with a lion's voice:

11. No, I have to end my life!
I never wanted to marry you,
It's not your fault if you kill my husband,
It's all because of lust for me!

When he heard these words, the king's passion for her disappeared, and then he recited another verse:

12. Live to your heart's content, fair lady,
Let's return to the top of Tuyet Son,
I know there are many animals
that eat only grass and flowers, and love wild forests.

With these words, the king calmly left. As soon as Candà knew that the king was gone, she stepped forward, hugged the Great Being, took him to the top of the hill and laid him down on a flat ground there; While placing his head on her lap, she lamented through the following twelve verses:

13. Here in the middle of the hills and peaks,
In many valleys, deep in caves,
What else should I do, my fairy,
Where can I see your shadow now?

14. Wild animals roam everywhere,
Leafs spread across many beautiful places,
What should I do, my dear Nguyet,
Because you are absent from this world now?

15. Wild beasts roam freely, fragrant flowers
Spread over many places of wild beauty,
What else should I do, my fairy,
Because there is nowhere to see your shadow?

16. Clear, many streams flowing along the hills,
Thousands of wildflowers, covering everywhere,
What should I do, young Moon,
Because now you leave me alone?

17. Deep blue are the Tuyet San hills and mountains.
When you look, the hills and mountains are incredibly beautiful.
What else should I do, my fairy,
Because I can't see your shadow anywhere?

18. The peaks of Snow Mountain are dyed golden,
Looking at the glorious mountains and hills,
What else should I do, my fairy,
Because where else can I see your shadow?

19. Snow Mountain hills are glowing red,
Mountains and hills are wonderful to look at!
What else should I do, my fairy,
Because where else can I see the fairy's shadow?

20. Snow Mountain's sharp peaks soar high into the sky,
How beautiful are the hills and mountains!
What will I do, my dear Nguyet,
Because I can't see you now?

21. Sparkling, Snow Mountain's white peak,
Look at the beautiful hills and mountains!
What else should I do, my fairy,
Because I can no longer see the Moon King?

22. Snow Mountain changes its rainbow color again,
It's wonderful to stand and watch!
What should I do, my dear Moon,
Because I can no longer see my husband?

23. Perfume Hill is close to demons,
Everywhere is covered with thousands of flowers and grass,
What should I do, young Moon,
Why can I still see Canda's shadow?
24. The fairies love Perfume Hill, 17
The trees and grass surround all the roads,
What will I do, my dear Moon,
Why can I still see the shadow of your love?

She kept complaining like that, then when she took the Great Master's hand and placed it on her chest, she saw that his hand was still warm. She thought to herself: "Canda is still alive, I am determined to provoke the gods until he is resurrected!". Then she loudly rebuked the gods:

- Is there no god who rules the earthly world? Where have you been traveling? You must all be dead, so there is no one left to save my beloved husband's life! Because of the power of her suffering, the throne of Sakka (Indra) became hot. When he looked closely, he clearly saw the reason, so he disguised himself as a Brahmin and approached her, holding a bottle of magical water and sprinkling it on the Great Being's body. In a moment, the poison lost its effectiveness, his face became bright again, and he no longer knew anything about the injury. The Great Master stood up completely recovered.

When Candà saw that her beloved husband was completely at peace, she joyfully knelt down at the feet of Thich Thich Thien, praising him through verses:

25. Saint La Mon is worthy of honor!
For this poor concubine
To see my husband full of love,
Sprinkling him with the holy medicine to revive him!

Then Thich Thich Thien advised:

He repeated this sentence twice and then returned to his realm. And Candà asked her husband:

- Hey husband, why are we in this dangerous place? Let's quickly return to the top of Nguyet Son.

Then she recited the last verse:

25. Let's retreat to the top of Moon San,
Where the beautiful stream flows,
The stream is covered with flowers and leaves,
Forever there, the gentle wind
Whispering through thousands of ancient trees,
Engaged in conversation, moments of peace.

* * *

When the Master finished this Dharma talk, He said: - Not only now, but also in the past, the Princess is always devoted and loyal to Me.

Then He recognized the Predecessor:

- At that time, Anuruddha (Anuruddha) was the king, Rahula's mother (Ràhulamàtà) was the fairy Candà and I was the male fairy.

Comment:

This is one of the most touching romances in the First Stories series.

According to classic legend, when the ascetic Sumedha (Thien Tue), the previous incarnation of Buddha Shakyamuni, was ordained by Ancient Buddha Dipankara (Nien Dang) to become a Buddha, there was a good woman who made a great vow to be his life partner for countless lifetimes until the day he attained Supreme Enlightenment.

This great vow was expressed through the faithful love between her and Bodhisattva, the Buddha's predecessor in many different forms: from a pair of pigeons, swans or crows, to a royal couple in the palace, she always highlighted her noble virtues alongside Bodhisattva throughout her life.

The Buddha told this Jataka story when he returned to Kapilavatthu to visit his family for the first time about five years after his enlightenment.

When he heard His father (Suddhodana: Sanskrit) praising the virtues of Princess Yasodhara, Venerable Rahula's mother, the Buddha confirmed that not only in this life, but through countless previous lives, in many forms of reincarnation, she had also remained faithful to Him and only wanted Him to guide her in life. This story is an example to prove that. Does His words imply that through countless past lives, she has fulfilled her noble vow of supporting the Bodhisattva in all situations of life on the path to seek the truth through all paths of reincarnation. Up to now, that mission has been completed, He has attained Supreme Enlightenment and become a Master guiding all beings in the heavens and human realms, so she should also follow the path he discovered to be enlightened and escape life and death like Him?

(Excerpt from the monthly magazine Giac Ngo, No. 82, January 2003)

(No. 387- Suci's predecessor)

Once upon a time, when King Brahmadatta (Pham Tho) ruled in Benares (Ba La Nai), Bodhisattva 20 was born in the land of Kàsi (Ca Thi) in the house of a blacksmith and when he grew up, he was very skilled in this profession. His parents were very poor. Not far from this village there is another village consisting of a thousand houses. The head of this union of thousands of blacksmiths was a man who had the king's favor and was rich in wealth and influence. This woman's daughter is extremely beautiful, just like a goddess, with all the good qualities of a good lady. Many people from surrounding villages came to help forge swords, axes, plowshares, sharp sticks... all saw her...

When they returned to the village, they praised her beauty in places where men gathered and many other places. Just hearing about her, the Bodhisattva felt infatuated and thought to himself: "I will marry her." Therefore, he chose the best iron and made a very hard and thin needle that could pierce the dice and float on water. Then he made a cover around it with that iron and also pierced the die with that bag of needles.

In this way, he made seven bags of gold, the method by which he made them is not revealed, because it was accomplished thanks to his great wisdom and understanding. Then he put the needle in the tube and put the tube in a box. He went into the other village and asked for directions to the house of the head of the blacksmith's guild. Then standing at the door of that house, he asked:

-- Who wants to buy this special metal rod from me in exchange for money?

And just standing next to the house of the head of the blacksmith's ward, he recited the first verse describing the needle:

1. Threads quickly, smoothly, straightly
Glued with green abrasive powder,
The tip of the needle is sharp and elegant,
Here is the needle, who wants to buy it?

Then he praised the needle again through the second verse:

2. The thread is fast, strong, straight,
The body of the well-trained needle is beautifully round!
That iron will also penetrate.
Here is the needle! Who wants to buy it?

At that time the girl was fanning her father with a palm leaf fan while he lay on a bamboo bed to get comfortable after breakfast. When she heard the Bodhisattva's sweet voice, she felt nauseous as if swallowing a piece of raw meat, and having to make that discomfort disappear with a thousand kettles of water, she said: -- Who could sell gold with such a sweet voice in a blacksmith village? What did he come here for? We have to find out what's going on.

So she put down the fan and went out to talk to him outside, standing in the hallway. The Bodhisattvas' goals are always achieved: it was because of her that he came to this village. She told him:

-- Hey, people in the country all come to this village to buy needles and similar items. And you want to sell metal in the blacksmith village, which is crazy! Even if you praise your products all day long, no one will buy your products! If you want a good price, go to another village. Then she recited two verses:

3. I have already sold the hooks,
No one knows about the village above, the lower village,
My blacksmith lives in this city,
Who else can sell sewing needles?

4. Our blacksmithing profession is famous,
Who can compare to making tools?
My blacksmith lives in the village,
Who still sells metal to us?

The Bodhisattva listened to her and quickly replied:

-- Lady, you say that because you don't understand anything.

Then he recited the next two verses:

5. Blacksmiths are all over the city,
But only talented people can sell their own metal!
The master of the craft is at hand,
Buy the best item right away so you don't miss it!

6. Once the strict father knows
This needle was made by me,
Your Majesty will definitely bestow
her fortune and karma on me.

The head of the blacksmith ward heard the whole story, then called his daughter in and asked: -- Are you talking to someone?

-- Father, a boy who sells metal.

-- Then call him in here.

She came out and called him in. The father respectfully greeted the forging ward leader and stood aside. He asked:

-- Which village are you from?

-- Dear sir, I live in that village, the son of that blacksmith family.

-- Why did you come here?

-- Dear, to sell needles.

-- Come on, let me see your needle.

The Bodhisattva wished to proclaim all his characteristics among many people, so he said:

-- Isn't it better for an object to be seen by many people than to be seen by just one person?

-- Hey man, that's true.

So, the village chief gathered all the blacksmiths together, and standing in the middle of the crowd, he said:

-- Come on man, get the needle out.

-- Dear sir, please tell me to bring out an anvil and a copper plate filled with water.

It is done immediately. Bodhisattva took the needle out of the box and showed it to the others. The head of the forging ward took it and asked:

-- Is this a needle?

-- No, that's not a needle, it's a sheath. The ward chief observed closely and could not see anything. Bodhisattva took it back, used his fingernail to pull out the bag and showed it to everyone:

-- This is a needle, this is a sheath.

He placed the needle in the ward chief's hand and the bag at his feet. The ward chief said again:

-- I'm sure this is a needle.

He replied:

-- This is just a bag of needles.

Then he used his hook to knock it out and just like that he placed six bags in a row at the feet of the ward chief and said:

-- This is a needle, and put the needle in the other person's arm.

Thousands of blacksmiths snapped their fingers with excitement and began waving their scarves in praise. Then the ward chief asked:

-- Hey man, how powerful is this needle?

-- Dear sir, please ask a strong man to tilt this anvil up and place a basin of water under the anvil. Then insert the needle straight into the anvil.

He said to do exactly that and inserted the sharp end of the needle into the anvil. The needle pierced the anvil and lay horizontally on the water's surface without moving up or down even by a hair.

All the blacksmiths said in unison:

-- We have never heard, not even through rumor, that there are blacksmiths like this!

Like that, they snapped their fingers and waved thousands of scarves.

The ward chief called his daughter in, and standing in the middle of the crowd, he said:

-- This is the girl who matches you. He immediately poured the water of commitment into their hands and gave her to him to take away.

Later, when the ward chief passed away, Bodhisattva became the head of the forging ward in that village.

When the dharma talk ended, the Master proclaimed the Noble Truths and identified his predecessors: "At that time, the daughter of the head of the blacksmith ward was mother Rahula 21, the intelligent blacksmith was me."

COMMENT:

This is a precursor story drawn from volume III, chapter 6 with six verses.

At a meeting at the Dharma Hall, the monks praised the Buddha's supreme perfect wisdom and presented that topic to him. Then, at your request, He told this story of the past to demonstrate His special and extraordinary wisdom in previous lives.

In that previous incarnation, the Bodhisattva was just a poor blacksmith in a lowly position in society, but thanks to his unusual intelligence, he accomplished a feat of making a needle with special power in six bags of needles. When pulled out, the needle was able to pierce the anvil and stand upright on the water in front of the admiration of all the blacksmiths, and then Bodhisattva was married by the head of the blacksmithing ward to the beautiful daughter who once made all the boys dream, among them Bodhisattva. That girl was the predecessor of the Venerable Rahula's mother, often called Princess Yasodharà (Da Du Da La). According to the classic tradition, when the Bodhisattva was still the ascetic Sumedha and was predicted to become a Buddha at the feet of Buddha Dìpankara (Nien Dang), there was a good woman who vowed to be the Bodhisattva's life partner through countless lives of birth and death until he attained Supreme Enlightenment. Later, she herself was inspired by His teachings and attained Arhatship.

The extraordinary good relationship between the Bodhisattva and his mother Rahula was one of the main themes of the previous series of stories and this story is a proven example. On the occasion of the beginning of the New Year of the Snake, I would like to send you an ancient story, clearly stating the extraordinary wisdom of the Bodhisattva in the previous incarnation of the Buddha, embedded in a strange relationship between a talented and talented couple full of romantic and poetic features, describing a lovesick boy who fell passionately in love even though he had not yet met the girl, which is a characteristic very suitable for eternal human love and has brought gentle joy to students of the Dharma throughout the ages.

(Excerpt from the monthly magazine Giac Ngo, No. 59, February 2001)
