noi_dung:
The Story of Evil

(No. 396. Precursor Kukku)

"The roof of this house is one and a half meters high..."

The Master told this story while staying at Jetavana about advising a king. This situation will appear in the Jataka
Tesakuna, no. 521.

Once upon a time, when King Brahmadatta reigned in Ba La Nai, Bodhisattva was the national teacher of worldly affairs as well as sacred affairs. That king followed an evil religion, ruled unjustly and accumulated wealth by oppressing the people. Bodhisattva wanted to advise the king, so he went around looking for an example.

At that time, the interior of the palace had not yet been completed, so the roof above was not complete. The rafters supporting the pointed roof have only just been placed in the correct position. The king was traveling in the royal garden. When he returned to the palace, he looked up and saw the round roof. Fearing it would fall, he stood outside, then looked up again and thought: "How does this roof stand so still? What are the rafters like?"

The king immediately recited the first verse and asked the Bodhisattva:

1. The roof of this house is one and a half meters high,
Eight large rafters support it
Made of sim-sa and sa-ra22,
So is the roof stable?

Hearing that, the Bodhisattva thought: "I have an example to advise the king." He immediately recited the following verses:

2. Thirty small sara wooden rafters
Arranged around the bottom of the roof,
Pressed together and lifted firmly,
So the roof stood straight.

3. So the wise person is gathered
With a wise national teacher, a loyal friend,
Will not fall into trouble at the end of his fortune,
Like a rafter supporting a stable roof.

While the Bodhisattva was speaking, the king carefully considered his behavior: "If there is no roof, the rafters cannot stand; the roof cannot stand without the support of the rafters. If the rafters break, the roof collapses. In the same way, an evil king does not gather together his relatives, ministers, army, Brahmans and householders, and if his servants disintegrate, the king cannot support will lose all power, so the king must live righteously."

At that moment, the maids brought a grapefruit to the king. The king told the Bodhisattva:

-- Hey friend, eat this grapefruit.

The Bodhisattva held a grapefruit and said:

-- Your Majesty, anyone who does not know how to eat grapefruit will make it bitter or spicy. But wise people know how to take out the bitter substances, and not remove the sour substances, or spoil the flavor of grapefruit when eating grapefruit.

Then using this example, he presented to the king how to create true wealth through two verses:

4. Eat the grapefruit with the bitter peel,
If you don't peel it with this knife,
Eat only the intestines and it will be fragrant and sweet,
If you add the peel, the sweetness will stop immediately.

5. So a wise person is not cruel
Collects taxes in villages,
Increases wealth but does not commit crimes.
Walking the right path creates fame.

-- Dear friend, that lotus flower grows straight up without water polluting its color and fragrance.

The Bodhisattva immediately replied:

-- Your Majesty, a king must also be like that.

And he recited these verses to preach:

6. Like a lotus blooming in a lake

7. White roots, clear water for maintenance,
Beautiful flowers bloom under the sun
No dust, no mud.

8. So the virtuous person leads the way,
Skilled in gentleness, good-natured enough,
Like a lotus flower in that lake,
Mud does not stain the heart.

Comment:

Teaching kings how to rule the country is one of the important topics of the Jataka series. Dozens of long stories are built around this theme, not to mention short stories embedded in other topics scattered throughout the series. Right during the first time the Buddha went to preach the Dharma to save living beings, he visited the Great King Bimbisara as promised before and preached to him and his officials at Rajagaha city. The king attained Stream-entry status and immediately made offerings to the Buddha's Veluvana monastery (Truc Lam) and became his loyal disciple.

Later, King Pasenadi of Kosala also came to the Buddha to listen to his sermon and became his lay disciple. The friendship between the Buddha and King Pasenadi that lasted for decades afterward created many favorable opportunities for him to preach to the king on many issues related to the home life of a king, and those sutras were compiled by the monks and included in the Samyutta Sutra with the title "Samyutta Kosala". This intimacy lasted until the last day of the king's life as described in the Dhammacetiya Sutra (Dhammacetiya Dharma, Central Sutra No. 89), before the king passed away the next morning.

The original scriptures also record the Buddha's reconciliation with many contemporary kings and princes such as King Udena, Ajatasattu, and a number of other monarchs. This proves that He is very interested in the lives of kings because they are the class that directly rules the country, and can bring happiness or suffering to the people depending on their way of thinking and acting. Especially through the Jataka Tales, we meet so many cruel kings who were encouraged by the Bodhisattva, the Buddha's previous incarnation, and the Bodhisattva always preached the Ten Kings Dharma to the kings and lords even though he was in the form of reincarnation as a bird, animal, or fairy, god, etc. For the Buddha, the Ten Kings Dharma (Dasa-ràjahammà) are the ten virtues of a wise king that any king must learn, which are (1) Giving alms, (2) Virtue, (3) Sacrifice, (4) Righteousness, (5) Kindness, (6) Temperance, (7) Non-anger, (8) Harmlessness, (9) Forbearance and (10) Not displeased with people. These virtues will enable the king to rule fairly and uprightly, taking the happiness of all people as the goal of his rule, and this will bring true happiness to the king himself in this life and the next.

As ​​in this Jataka story, the Bodhisattva taught that a good king must be supported by a group of good courtiers to be able to firmly sit on the throne. If the king is encouraged by his courtiers to do evil things, it will lead to the decline of that dynasty.

For the masses, the king does not enjoy unjust profits by imposing heavy taxes to avoid causing suffering and resentment to the people, just like when we eat grapefruit, we must leave the peel on to avoid tasting the bitter taste. In short, a king with a good reputation is like a lotus flower blooming fragrantly under the sun without dirt and dust.

Buddha's teachings to the country's leaders are practical and beneficial throughout the ages. This proves that He cares deeply about human social life and is willing to educate everyone in the right position of a true person in life to bring true happiness to himself and many others.

These characteristics of the Buddha's teachings on home life are in sharp contrast to the erroneous comments of some non-Buddhists who believe that the Buddha advocated staying away from life and did not want to have anything to do with the problems of secular life in society. The massive Jataka series with rich and diverse topics presents almost every aspect of human life: in addition to the practice of the monastic community, there are hundreds of other stories related to the activities of normal society with the aim of helping each person find peace and happiness according to their life's aspirations.

(Excerpt from the monthly magazine Giac Ngo, No. 67, October 2001)

tieu_de: Story of the Great Monkey King
tom_tat: Story of the Great Monkey King (No. 407. Mahàkapi's predecessor) "You yourself have crossed the monkey bridge …." The Master told this story while staying at Jetavana about good karma towards relatives. The circumstances of this story will appear in the Bhadda Jataka
noi_dung:
The Story of the Great Monkey King

(No. 407. Mahàkapi's predecessor)

"You yourself have crossed the monkey bridge …."

The Master told this story while staying at Jetavana about good karma towards relatives. The circumstances of this story will appear in Bhaddasāla No. 465.X. The monks began to discuss in the Dharma hall, saying to each other: "The omniscient Buddha has done many good deeds for his relatives." When the Master asked the Sangha and was presented with the above topic, he replied: "Monks, this is not the first time Tathagata has done good karma towards his relatives." And He told a story from the past.

Once upon a time, when King Brahmadatt reigned in Ba La Nai, Bodhisattva entered the womb of a monkey. When he grew up, he had a majestic and strong physique, living with a group of eighty thousand monkeys in Tuyet Son.

Near the banks of the Ganges River, there is a mango tree (many others say it is a banyan tree) with shady branches and dense leaves like a mountain peak. The sweet mango has a wonderful scent and taste, and is as big as water bottles. Fruit from one branch fell to the ground, from another branch fell into the Ganges River, from two other branches fell into the tree.

While eating mangoes with monkeys, the Bodhisattva thought to himself: "One day a disaster will happen to me because the mango fell into the water."

However, a ripe mango was hidden in an anthill, so the eighty thousand monkeys, unable to see it, fell into the river and got caught in the net above. King Ba La Nai was bathing in the river and having fun with a net above and a net below.

When the king had had fun all day and was about to leave in the evening, the fishermen were pulling up their nets, saw the fruit, but didn't know what kind of fruit, so they immediately brought it to the king. The King asked:

-- What fruit is that?

-- Your Majesty, we do not know.

-- So who knows?

-- Your Majesty, forest rangers.

The king called the rangers and when he heard them say it was a mango, the king took a knife and cut it out, then first told the rangers to eat the mango, then the king himself ate the mango. The flavor of ripe mango permeated the king's entire body. Due to his desire for the taste of captivity, the king asked the rangers where that tree was, and when he heard that the tree was on the riverbank toward Tuyet Son, the king ordered to assemble rafts and row upstream along the river following the route guided by the rangers. The exact number of days on the road is not stated.

Over time, they arrived at that place, and the rangers reported to the king:

-- Your Majesty, that is a mango tree.

The king stopped the raft and walked to the place with a large crowd of courtiers. Then he spread the bed and sat down right under the tree. The king lay down to sleep after eating mangoes and enjoying all kinds of wonderful flavors. On all sides, soldiers kept careful watch and lit fires. When everyone was asleep, Bodhisattva and the monkeys arrived there at midnight.

Eighty thousand monkeys passed from branch to branch eating mangoes. The king woke up and saw the monkeys, so he woke up his servants and called the gunners to say:

-- Surround the mango-eating monkeys so they can't escape, then shoot them all. Tomorrow I want to eat mango and monkey meat.

The gunners obeyed the order and responded in unison:

-- Thank you very much.

Then they surrounded the whole tree with bows and arrows at the ready. The monkeys saw them, were afraid of death because they could not escape, immediately jumped to the Bodhisattva and said:

-- My Lord, the gunners are surrounding the tree and saying: "I will shoot to death this wandering and thieving monkey." What should we do now? They stood and trembled.

Bodhisattva said:

-- Don't be afraid, I will save your lives.

Having comforted the monkeys like that, he climbed up a branch that grew vertically, then passed another branch stretching towards the Ganges River, then jumped again to the end of that branch, crossed a hundred arches and landed on a bush on the bank.

When he got there, he marked the distance and said: "That is the distance I have overcome." Then cut a bamboo shoot close to the root, peel the bark and say: "This part will be tied to that tree, and the other part will be in the air." When calculating these two lengths, he forgot the part tied to his belt. He held a bamboo shoot and tied one end to a tree trunk on the bank of the Ganges River and the other part to his waist, then jumped across that distance of one hundred arcs with the speed of clouds flying in the wind. 23.

Because he did not count the bamboo tied to his body, he could not reach that tree. So he grabbed the tree branch with both hands and signaled to the monkeys:

-- I wish you luck, come quickly, walk on my back along the bamboo tree.

All eighty thousand monkeys escaped that way, after respectfully bowing to the Bodhisattva and asking his permission to leave.

At that time Devadatta (Bodhidharma) was a monkey in that group, thinking to himself: "This is my opportunity to eliminate the enemy."

So as soon as it climbed the tree branch, it jumped and fell on Bodhisattva's back. Bodhisattva's heart was broken, extremely painful. After causing him such pain and suffering, it immediately left, leaving only Bodhisattva alone.

When morning came, the king rejoiced in the Bodhisattva and thought: "Killing this monkey lord is really not dharma, I want him to come down and take care of him." So the king turned the raft down to the Ganges River and built a high bridge there for the Bodhisattva to jump down gently. He ordered a yellow robe to be placed on his back and bathed him in the river, gave him sugar water to drink, wiped his body clean and soaked it in fragrant oil that had been filtered a thousand times. Then the king spread an oiled skin on the throne and placed him there, while the king lay in a lower place.

And the king recited the first verse:

It was you who crossed the monkey bridge
So the whole herd could escape safely,
Hey monkey, you and them are related,
Or what are they to you?

Hearing these words, the Bodhisattva recited verses to advise the king:

Your Majesty, I look after those people,
As the Monkey King, I control the whole herd,
Those people are full of terror,
Because of you, my heart is filled with sadness and pain.

I jumped over a hundred great arcs
Spread in a horizontal position,
Then when I tied the bamboo stick
Sturdyly around my side.

Wanting to reach the tree like the stormy moon,
The wind blew extremely fast,
But losing momentum, I only reached the tip of the branch,
Holding it, my hand was steady.

When I was hanging from the tree,
Tie tightly to the branch with a piece of young bamboo,
The monkeys had already walked with their backs bent,
Now they are safe to escape.

I am not afraid of the pain of death,
Even if I am imprisoned, I will not be sad,
When there is peace and happiness with the whole flock,
In the past, I ruled over them.

An example for you, the Great Emperor,
If you wish to learn true morality:
The joy and happiness of the entire people,
With the army, and the city with war horses.

All are dear to you,
If you wish to rule the country peacefully.

After the Bodhisattva taught the king like that, he immediately passed away. The king called his ministers to command the Monkey King to enjoy the funeral like a king. Then the king told his concubines:

-- Ladies, please take the Monkey King to the cemetery as the Monkey King's entourage, wearing red robes, hair down and holding torches in hand.

The ministers built a funeral pyre with a hundred carts of firewood. After preparing the Bodhisattva's funeral according to royal rites, they brought his striped bones to present to the king. The king ordered to build a temple at the site of Bodhisattva's cremation, hold a torch lighting ceremony and offer offerings of incense and flowers. The king again inlaid gold into the skull, raised it high on the tip of the spear and placed it at the city gate, then offered flowers and incense when the king arrived at Ba La Nai. Then he ordered the entire capital to be decorated solemnly, and the king held a ceremony to honor the relics for seven days.

After receiving the relics and building a temple in the city, the king went there to make offerings of flowers and incense for the rest of his life. Having relied on the Bodhisattva's teachings, the king focused on giving alms and doing many other good deeds and ruling righteously, so he was later reborn in Heaven.

COMMENT:

Love for relatives is also a common theme in the Tale of the Past.

In this case, that tragic vow was made in the presence of a king in the human world. This king was fond of having fun and loved delicious and strange things, so he and a group of officials rowed boats up to the Tuyet Son region to enjoy the rare mango dish. Therefore, the king ordered to kill all 80 thousand monkeys that came to compete for that delicacy. But those small creatures were Bodhisattva's subjects. Because they were afraid of death, they asked him for protection and he was willing to use his body as a means to help their fellow humans escape the king's arrows. Thus, all the monkeys were protected by him, but because of his adverse relationship with Devadatta, he had to sacrifice his life while completing the task of helping his fellow humans.

Afterwards, the king ordered a national funeral for the monkey king and the construction of a temple for his relics. Then, like the king in his previous incarnation, King Hoan Hy of Loc, this king was also imbued with the ethics of being a king, so he followed the Bodhisattva's advice and practiced the Ten virtues of a wise ruler who stands by the Dharma to bring true happiness to himself instead of concentrating on enjoying sensual pleasures as is the usual habit of kings in the world, and at the same time bringing happiness to the people through many good deeds, so after his death, the king was reborn in heaven according to the law of cause and effect of all things. object.

(Excerpt from the monthly magazine Giac Ngo, No. 61, April 2001)

noi_dung:
The story of King Susìma

(No. 411. Susìma's predecessor)

"My hair has been jet black since the old days..."

The Master told this story while staying at Jetavana about the Great Event
in the world. The Sangha at that time were sitting in the Dharma Hall praising the Great Birth of the Buddha. When he saw that this was your topic, He said: -- Monks, it is no wonder that today I am doing the great event of leaving the world and leaving the world, when I have practiced the perfect deeds (Paramitas) for hundreds of thousands of eons, and in the past I also gave up the throne in the land of Kàsi
three hundred yojanas (miles) wide and did the great event of leaving the world. And so, He told the
story of the past.

Once upon a time, when King Brahmadatta reigned in Ba La Nai, Bodhisattva entered the womb of the wife of the royal monk. On the day he was born, the queen also gave birth to a son. On the naming ceremony, the 24th Great Being was called Son Susìma, and the royal son was named King Brahmadatta.

The king saw that the young couple were born on the same day, so he entrusted the Bodhisattva to his nurse and raised them with the prince. Both children grew up as beautiful as angels in heaven.

Both studied all kinds of arts in Takkasilà and returned home. The prince became the viceroy, ate, drank, and lived with the Bodhisattva. When the father passed away, the prince became king, bestowed all glory on the Bodhisattva and conferred the title of Royal Priest.

One day the new king ordered the entire capital to be decorated, then brilliantly decorated like Sakka the Heavenly Master, the king participated in the procession around the capital, sitting on the shoulders of a royal statue like the Eràvana 25 statue of the Heavenly Lord, in pride with the Bodhisattva sitting behind on the back of an elephant. The mother looked out the window and saw the king and suddenly saw the priest behind the king when he returned from the procession. She fell in love with him, so she went into the harem and thought to herself: "If I don't capture him, I will die here."

The king didn't see his mother and immediately asked about her. When he heard that she was sick, he came to visit and respectfully asked her what was wrong. She didn't speak because she was ashamed. The king immediately sat on the throne and ordered the queen to find out what was wrong with the queen mother.

The Queen came, asked questions, and caressed her mother's back. Women usually don't keep secrets from each other, so the secret was revealed. The queen immediately went to report to the king. He said:

-- Dear friend, please save my mother's life, you will become king and my mother will become chief queen, and I will become viceroy. The Priest replied:

-- Impossible.

But after being repeatedly begged, he agreed and the king crowned him king, his mother as chief queen and himself as viceroy. Everyone lives in harmony, but the Bodhisattva withers leads the lay life. He abandoned all sensual pleasures and turned to a life of practice.

No longer caring about worldly pleasures, he walked, stood, and sat like a prisoner under house arrest or a rooster in a red cage. The Queen thought: "The Emperor avoids me. He walks, stands, and sits alone. Now he is still young, while I am old and have gray hair. Suppose I tell him the story that he has gray hair, making him believe it and come to keep me company?"

One day, as if wiping the king's head, she said:

-- Your Majesty is getting old, there is a gray hair on His head!

-- Spit it out and put it in my hand.

The queen pulled out a strand of hair, but threw it away and placed a strand of her silver hair in his hand. When he saw it, the fear of death caused sweat to flow down his forehead, even though his forehead was as shiny as a slab of gold, he said to himself: "Hey Susìma, you are old in your youth, all this time you have been sinking deep into the mud of sensual pleasures like a countryside pig diving in the mud, you cannot stay away from the mud. Leave desire and desire, and live an ascetic life in the Snow Mountains. Now is the time to become a monk." Along with this idea, he recited the first verse:

My hair is jet black from the past
Still grows around my forehead,
It's white now, pay attention;
It's time for me to step away.

This is my gray hair, it's not you,
I brought it from above,
Because of you, I said false things,
Please forgive me for my mistakes,
You look beautiful and elegant
Like a young tree in the middle of spring,
Rule your country, smile at me,
Don't look for work in autumn and winter!

Song Bodhisattva replied:

-- Hey Queen, the Queen is talking about things that must happen: When age is ripe, this black hair must turn silver like lime, we see the deterioration of the body over the years when it comes to old age, from the princess to everyone else, even though they are as soft as a green lotus flower, bright and beautiful as pure gold, and intoxicated with the pride of their brilliant youth. Hey queen, that is the terrible end of all sentient beings.

Furthermore, wanting to present the truth with the power of a Buddha, he recited two verses:

I often see young girls in their prime,
Elegant like those graceful branches,
Arrogant because of the beautiful image,
Everyone watches her footsteps in awe.

It's the same girl I've been looking at
(For eight, ninety years)
Trembling on her feet, holding a cane in her hand,
Her body is bent like a shaking willow.

In this verse, the Great Being clearly states the suffering of form and now declares his dissatisfaction with the lay life:

I consider these thoughts all the time,
Thinking still comes in the middle of a lonely night,
I don't like worldly life,
At the right time to practice, I have to step in,
Less pleasure in the life of the worldly person
Is a weak place to take refuge,
The human mind cuts it off, follows another path,
Abandon other sensual pleasures with divine power.

Thus, while proclaiming both the pleasures and sufferings of desire, he expounded the truth with the magic of the Enlightened One, then he invited his friends to reclaim the kingdom: He said goodbye to glory and power amid the wailing of his relatives and friends, became an ascetic sage in the Snow Mountain region, and later attained Zen, he was reborn in the Brahma world.

When the Dharma talk ended, the Master proclaimed the Noble Truths and brought immortal water to many people. He identified his predecessor: At that time, the chief queen was mother Rahula, the king was Ānanda and king Susìma was me.

COMMENTS

The great event of the birth is the most important topic in the mountain of Jataka stories. Through countless lives of birth and death, the Bodhisattva repeatedly left the world to become a hermit to practice. He could leave from any situation: untouchable, rich man, Brahmin or king.

Especially in this previous life, following the earnest request of the king who was his close friend to save the queen mother from a hopeless love affair, the Bodhisattva reluctantly matched the queen mother and became the king beside his friend. He voluntarily became vice king.

Living in the midst of a luxurious life of supreme power and fame with that eternal royal love, the Bodhisattva did not feel happy, so he gradually abandoned desire and turned his mind to a life of solitary practice.

According to the story of a strand of gray hair appearing in the middle of his youth, he decided that this was the time for him to become a monk and leave the world. He explained to the queen the impermanent law of all things: a form of existence in this world will one day perish and will bring suffering to those who only want to cling to the sensual pleasures of that fleeting body until it is too late, there is no time left to practice the body and mind to prepare to enter the afterlife.

That was the problem that haunted his mind, constantly making him uneasy in his home life, and in the end, with the sword of wisdom, he resolutely cut off his desires, returned the throne to his friend and left amid the cries of his relatives. He became a hermit practicing meditation in the Snow Mountain region until he attained Zen attainments and was reborn in the Brahma world.

It is difficult to say goodbye to glory and power between youth and renunciation, from the attachment of friends and relatives. But that is something that the Bodhisattva regularly did through countless reincarnations until his final life. He reappeared in the world as a crown prince in King Tinh Phan's palace and lived at home. However, he was always pondering about the problem of human birth and death and he wanted to find a solution to that problem, so he finally left home in the middle of his youth to find the truth of liberation and enlightenment for all living beings.

How rare is the great birth of kings in this world, especially in their youth. However, in our country in the 13th century, there was King Tran Nhan Tong who followed the Buddha's great example and practiced his wish to become a monk; After twice defeating foreign invaders and passing the throne to his son, he went to Yen Tu Mountain to practice asceticism and became the First Patriarch of Truc Lam, starting a brilliant career of spreading Zen Buddhism in the history of Vietnamese Buddhism, bringing great honor to Vietnamese Buddhists for generations to come.

(Excerpt from the monthly magazine Giac Ngo, No. 62, May 2001)

noi_dung:
The Story of Sage Mother Kaccàni

(No. 417. Precursor Kaccàni)

"Wearing a white shirt and shoulder-length hair..."

The Master told this story while staying at Jetavana about a person who took care of his mother.

One day this lay person came to Ky Vien to listen to the Dharma, and after bowing to the Master, he stood to one side. The Master asked if he still did not neglect his old duties, and was still devoted to taking care of his old mother.

He replied:

-- Yes, World-Honored One. Your mother brought you a girl to be your wife against your will. She did many unworthy things.

Then he told Him everything:

-- But she can't separate your mother from you, so now she takes care of her very respectfully.

The Master heard the story and said:

-- Nowadays he does not listen to his wife, but in the past he left his mother because he listened to his wife's instigation and asked me to bring her back home for him to take care of.

Then at his request, He told a story from the past.

Once upon a time, when King Brahmadatta ruled in Ba La Nai, there was a young man in a family who wholeheartedly took care of his old mother when his father passed away. Just like the fate of this story, the details are also fully stated as above. But in this case, when the wife said she couldn't live with that woman and he had to decide one of them had to leave, he followed his wife's words and said that his mother was at fault and said:

-- Mom, you always fight in this house, from now on you can go live somewhere else as you please.

The mother heard that, cried and went to a friend's house somewhere, working as a hired laborer, struggling to make ends meet. After she left, her daughter-in-law became pregnant and gave birth to a son, so she often told her husband and neighbors that such a birth had never happened before when she was still in the house.

So one day, she brought ground sesame, rice, a small pot and spoon, she went to the cemetery to light a fire in a furnace made of three human skulls, then she went down to the stream to wash her head, washed her clothes, returned to the fire, let her hair down and began washing rice. At that time, the Bodhisattva was Lord Sakka 26, and the Bodhisattvas were always alert. At that moment, He looked down at the world and saw that poor old woman holding a burial ceremony for Than Cong Chanh as if Than Cong Chanh had died. Wanting to prove his power in helping her, he descended to earth disguised as a Brahmin traveling on the road; When he saw her, he left the main road to stand next to her, starting the story by asking:

-- Mom, people usually don't cook rice in cemeteries. What do you plan to do with this rice and sesame when it's finished cooking?

Then he recited the first verse:

1. Wearing a white shirt and her hair hanging down her shoulders,
Kac-ca-ni boiled the pot again,
The sesame rice you washed over there,
Did you use it when it was cooked?

She recited the second verse to tell him:

2. Dear Taoist, I don't want to eat,
Ground sesame and even stewed rice:
Now that the God of Cong Chanh is dead,
I want to make offerings to him.

God, the incarnation of the God of Justice, responded to the third verse:

3. When making a decision, she must think:
Who did you hear saying such false words?
That thousand-eyed person27 is so powerful,
The God of Justice cannot die.

Listening to what he said, the old woman recited the next couple of verses:

4. La Mon, I witnessed clearly,
"Justice is dead" I have to believe:
All those who follow evil deeds
are now enjoying great prosperity.

5. My daughter-in-law was rare in the past,
beat me, then gave birth to a son,
He became the mistress of the house,
I was forgotten, abandoned.

God Sakka immediately recited the sixth verse:

6. No, I will live forever,
Now I come to this world, because of you,
Your daughter-in-law beat her mother, her daughter-in-law, and her grandchildren
Will turn to ashes in my fire.

Hearing that, the old woman cried out loudly:

-- Alas, what did you just say? I will do my best to keep my nephew from dying.

Then she recited the seventh verse:

7. Heavenly Lord, I hope it will be according to your wishes,
For me, you come from heaven,
Wishing the young couple and the grandchild,
To live a life of harmony with me.

Then Lord Sakka recited the eighth verse:

8. Kati28 will be satisfied, because I
was beaten, but she believed in me
Justice, so with her children and grandchildren
Live a peaceful life at home.

-- Kaccàni, don't be afraid, thanks to my divine power, your son and daughter-in-law will come here to take you home; live in harmony with them.

Then he returned to his realm.

Thanks to the power of God, her son and daughter-in-law thought of all her good qualities in the past and searched throughout the village. They found her walking towards the cemetery. They followed that path and called her. When they met her again, they knelt down at her feet to apologize and were forgiven for their old mistakes.

She happily welcomed her grandson. So they all happily returned home and from then on lived together.

9. With her daughter-in-law following, she happily
The old woman Ka-ti lived together,
God reconciled the old conflict,
Her grandchildren took care of her very attentively.

This verse was inspired by the Supreme Wisdom of the Buddha.

After the Dharma talk, the Master proclaimed the Noble Truths and identified the Precursors: -- At the end of the Noble Truths, the layperson is placed in the first stage of Stream-entry. At that time, the lay person who took care of his mother was the one taking care of his mother today, the wife of that time was the wife of today, and Sakka the Lord of Heaven was me.

Comment:

This is a Zen story related to the filial piety of a lay disciple of the Buddha.

We have read Jataka stories related to the filial piety of some Bhikkhus whose elderly parents needed to take care of them, and that was also approved by the Buddha. As for lay disciples, filial piety was raised by the Buddha as one of their top duties.

However, in this story, Buddha tells about an ungrateful son who was transformed by his old mother's immense love for her children and grandchildren. Here, that poor, gentle old mother was cruelly kicked out of the house by her son and daughter-in-law, so she thought that the God of Justice had died and she went to the cemetery to bury the Supreme God. This scene touched the heart of Sakka, the God of Justice in heaven, when he looked down at the earthly world.

He wanted to prove that he was still alive to help good people in trouble like the old woman and punish evil people like her daughter-in-law in accordance with the fair law of Karma. But that old mother was a kind and generous mother, so she quickly asked God to forgive her daughter-in-law's sins and only wanted to live in harmony with her children and grandchildren, not wanting him to punish them.

On the occasion of the Lan King's Day - the season of the Leopard, I would like to send to my friends near and far this story of the Predecessor, imbued with human love mixed with religious flavor. The content of the story clearly shows the immense love of a gentle mother and also of countless gentle mothers in the world who are always ready to generously forgive all their children's mistakes and only wish happiness for their children and grandchildren no matter what situation they are in, no matter how much they have to endure all the disadvantages.

(Excerpt from the monthly magazine Giac Ngo, No. 65, August 2001)

tom_tat: The Story of the Leopard (No. 426. Dìpi's predecessor) "Uncle, are you in peace..." The Master told this story while staying at Ky Vien about a female goat. Once the Elder Moggallàna lived in a hermitage with one door, in a land surrounded by fences and mountains
noi_dung:
The Story of the Leopard

(No. 426. Former Dìpi)

"Uncle, may you be in peace..."

The Master told this story while staying at Jetavana about a female goat.

Once Elder Moggallàna lived in a hermitage with one door, in a land surrounded by fences and mountains. The covered walkway of his house is near that door. Some shepherds thought that fence was a good place for goats, so they drove their goats there and lived comfortably. One day they came in the afternoon and took the whole herd of goats away. But one female goat wandered too far and did not see the goats leave, and was left alone. Then when he left, a leopard saw him and wanted to eat him, so he stood by the door of the fence. The female goat looked around and saw the leopard. "The leopard stood there because it wanted to kill me and eat me." The goat thought: "If I turn around and run, I will lose my life. So I have to be brave." Then the goat raised its horns and ran straight in front of the leopard with all its strength. The goat escaped the leopard's claws, although the leopard trembled because it thought it would catch the goat. Then running at full speed, the goat caught up with the herd.

The Elder observed how the animals treated each other. The next day he went to report to the Tathagata:

-- World-Honored One, the female goat achieved a feat thanks to her strategy and escaped the leopard.

The Master replied:

-- Hey Moggallàna, this time the leopard couldn't catch the goat, but in the past the leopard killed the goat even though the goat cried loudly, and then ate it. And at the request of the Venerable Moggallàna, He told a story from the past.

Once upon a time, a Bodhisattva was born in a village in Magadha, into a rich family. When he grew up, he gave up lust and lived a life of practice, achieving perfect meditation. After living for a long time in Tuyet Son, he went to Rajagàha to find salt and vinegar, then returned to reside in the hermitage he built in a fenced valley.

Like in the part of dependent origination, the shepherds herd the goats out and like above, one day, when a female goat went out slower than the other herd, a leopard waited at the door, thinking of a way to eat it. When the goat saw the leopard, he thought: "My life is over; by some trick I must lure it into a cheerful and considerate conversation to soothe its heart and save my life." While standing at a distance, he started talking friendly with the bag and goat, reciting the first verse:

Dear uncle, are you in good health?
And have you been healthy for a long time?
My mother sent a message to ask respectfully,
I hope to become friends with you!

Hearing this, the leopard thought: "This girl wants to deceive me by calling me 'uncle'; she doesn't know how fierce I am." Therefore, the second verse is recited:

You stepped on my tail, little goat,
And hurt me so much,
I thought that by calling me 'uncle',
You were free to return!

When he heard that, the goat replied:

-- Sir, please don't say that.

And it recites the third verse:

I'm walking in front, sir,
You're still sitting there facing me,
Your tail is behind that side,
How can I lift it?

Response:

-- Hey goat, what are you talking about? Is there any place that doesn't have my tail spread out?

And it recites the fourth verse:

Throughout the four great continents,
With its rivers, lakes, seas and high mountains,
My tail spreads far and wide,
Why don't the goat's legs step on it?

When she heard this, the goat thought: "This evil beast is not seduced by sweet words. So I will respond to it as an enemy." Then the goat recited the fifth verse:

I know the evil man's tail is very long,
Because I have been informed,
My parents all advised me,
I was flying in the sky before!

Snooze says:

-- I know you flew in the sky. But when you arrived you ruined my bait by landing!

Then recite the sixth verse:

The silhouette of the goat girl in the sky
Flying through the air alone,
It frightened the deer,
So our bait was ruined!

Hearing this, I was afraid of death and could no longer find any other excuse, so I shouted loudly:

-- Uncle, please don't commit such a cruel thing, please spare my life.

But even though the goat cried loudly, the leopard still grabbed its shoulder, killed and ate the goat.

It is the goat that cries loudly to ask for favor,
But it is the flesh and blood that is satisfied,
The wild beast grabs the goat by the throat;
The wicked do not show any kindness.

Evil people do not know how to show
kindness, righteousness, avoid evil ways,
They hate good people,
The best policy is to fight hand to hand!

These are two verses derived from the Supreme Wisdom (of the Buddha)

An ascetic Saint witnessed all the stories of these two beasts.

Comment:

This is a Precursor story related to things that often happen in life: the strong win, the weak lose.

Strong people with evil intentions often use absurd excuses to oppress those weaker than themselves and then destroy the victims without mercy.

The goat here symbolizes weak people who often lose out in life and sometimes lose their lives. But if it has the determination to rise up against the large and aggressive enemy, it can escape and succeed.

Bodhisattva is an ascetic sage who witnessed firsthand the courage and success of the goat and praised the goat for its efforts to defend itself against a cruel enemy who did not know what was right. He then advised people in similar situations, "the best policy is to fight hand-to-hand" to have a chance of survival, otherwise the weak must be destroyed, which is inevitable according to the law of survival among all species.

The Jataka Tale of the Buddha is a cultural treasure that harmoniously combines the Buddha's teachings and folk legends. Many stories related to moral conduct in life have been passed down through the ages and have crossed the Indian border to spread everywhere with a profound influence on many literatures around the world.

In the 17th century in France, there was the poet La Fontaine (1621-1695) famous for his Fables (Les Fables). La Fontaine admitted that he took materials from Greek, Roman and Indian fairy tales to create fables and he emphasized: His moral purpose was "to use animals to teach humanity". He saw himself as continuing the moral teaching tradition of the ancient fables who used simple, entertaining stories to admonish humans on proper behavior. Therefore, his fables were gradually translated into many languages ​​around the world, and in our country, these stories were translated into Vietnamese poetry for the first time by scholar Nguyen Van Vinh and have since been included in textbooks at primary and secondary school levels. We see that many of these stories have similar content to the previous stories, such as the story of the Frog wanting to be as big as a cow, the Wolf and the Sheep, etc. In particular, the story 'The Wolf and the Sheep' has a dialogue between the two animals similar to the words of the leopard and the goat here: the wolf accuses the sheep of clouding its stream water before pouncing on the sheep to eat it.

Thus, it is clear that La Fontaine found inspiration in ancient Indian folk tales to build modern fables according to his creativity while still retaining a special traditional feature of ancient fables: the personification of animals so that they can dialogue with each other and thereby contain the true concept of living in life. Thanks to such a flexible, gentle and interesting method of teaching morality, these fables have been spread throughout the world, and we can say that the moral lessons of the Jatakas have had a direct or indirect influence all over the world throughout the ages.

(Excerpt from the monthly magazine Giac Ngo, No. 64, July 2001)
